examples.question_text: A machine part passes inspection on $89\%$ of checks. One part is checked. Let $X=1$ if the part fails inspection and $X=0$ otherwise. State the success and failure events, then write the Bernoulli model for $X$.
examples.solution_text:
Success: the part fails inspection. Failure: the part passes inspection.

$\begin{aligned}p&=P(X=1)\\&=1-0.89\\&=0.11\end{aligned}$

$X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(0.11)$

examples.question_text: A seed germinates with probability $0.72$. One seed is planted. Let $X=1$ if it germinates and $X=0$ otherwise. Write the Bernoulli model and find $E(X)$, $\text{Var}(X)$ and $\sigma(X)$. Give the standard deviation correct to three decimal places.

examples.solution_text:
Multiply the probabilities of the outcomes in the stated order.

(a) $\begin{aligned}P(\text{score, score})&=0.65\times0.65\\&=0.4225\end{aligned}$

(b) $\begin{aligned}P(\text{miss})&=1-0.65\\&=0.35\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}P(\text{score, score, miss, miss})&=0.65^2\times0.35^2\\&=0.05175625\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A biased coin shows heads with probability $0.4$. A student tosses it $12$ times and writes $X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(0.4)$, where $X$ is the number of heads. Explain why this is not a Bernoulli model, then define a correct Bernoulli variable for this coin.
examples.solution_text:
The number of heads over $12$ tosses can take values from $0$ to $12$. A Bernoulli variable describes one trial and takes only the values $0$ and $1$.

For one toss, define $Y=1$ if the coin shows heads and $Y=0$ if it shows tails.

$Y\sim\text{Bernoulli}(0.4)$

examples.derivation: Failure to pass is the defined success, so p=1−0.89=0.11. The single binary trial therefore has X∼Bernoulli(0.11), matching the booklet's complementary-event modelling method.
For the single seed, p=0.72. E(X)=0.72 and Var(X)=0.72×0.28=0.2016. Independently taking the square root gives σ(X)=0.448998886…, which rounds to 0.449 to three decimal places.

Independence gives P(score, score)=0.65²=0.4225. The miss probability is 0.35, so the specified four-throw order has probability 0.65²×0.35²=0.4225×0.1225=0.05175625. No arrangements factor applies to a specified order. Both tasks follow the supplied multistage-probability review.

The count of heads across 12 tosses has possible values 0 through 12, so it is not a binary Bernoulli variable. For one toss, Y=1 for heads and Y=0 for tails gives P(Y=1)=0.4 and Y∼Bernoulli(0.4), following the booklet's single-toss versus repeated-count contrast.
